title: India's AM Intelligence orders 9,000 Nvidia Vera Rubin systems for a Hyderabad AI factory
subtitle: The Greenko-linked startup is committing more than $8 billion in capex to build a 1 GW cross-border compute footprint anchored on low-cost renewable power.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: AM Intelligence, an Indian AI-infrastructure company founded by the promoters of renewable-energy producer Greenko Group, has placed a binding order for 9,000 Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale systems. Delivery is scheduled for the first quarter of 2027 and the first cluster will land at the company's Hyderabad AI data centre. The order was disclosed on August 25, 2026 in Bloomberg's reporting and confirmed the same day by AM Intelligence's own statements to Indian trade press.

The order matters because it puts AM Intelligence in the earliest Vera Rubin shipping cohort — a slot that, until now, has effectively been reserved for US hyperscalers, sovereign programs, and a small circle of neoclouds. Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform is the successor to Blackwell, and NVL72 rack-scale systems are the same form factor that OpenAI, Microsoft, and Oracle have booked for their 2027 deployments. Hyderabad becoming a first-wave site rather than a follow-on one is the news.

The company plans to build 1 GW of AI compute across India, the United States, Finland, and Malaysia, backed by more than $8 billion in capital expenditure, and is targeting 5 GW of data-centre capacity by 2030. The stated pitch is a global token economics one: energy prices are now the dominant variable in inference cost, and Greenko's access to cheap renewable power in Andhra Pradesh gives AM Intelligence a structural discount that most competitors can't match. That thesis is what turned a two-year-old startup into a nine-figure Nvidia customer.

For learners: the story of AI in the next 24 months will not be told at the model layer alone. Where the electrons come from — and at what price per kilowatt-hour — is now a first-order determinant of which countries can host serious inference workloads. Watching the map of new data-centre commitments (India, Finland, the US Gulf Coast, Malaysia, Norway, Saudi) is a faster way to see where AI economic power is shifting than watching any leaderboard.
